column1: # title: ENG-205 Middle Ages Intro — 4 Main Ideas
When the Middle Ages began and ended, and its three sub-periods
column2: The Middle Ages run from around 450, when Rome left Britain and the Anglo-Saxons arrived, to around 1485, when the Tudors, the Renaissance and printing arrived. The literature of the period falls into three sub-periods: Anglo-Saxon, Anglo-Norman and Middle English.

column1: How the Norman Conquest of 1066 changed language in England
column2: The Norman Conquest of 1066 put a French-speaking elite on top, and four languages then circulated: French for the court and law, Latin for the Church and learning, English for the common people, and the Celtic languages. English sank for about 200 years, then came back as Middle English full of French words, and by 1362 it was used in the law courts and Parliament.

column1: The main features of Old English poetry
column2: Old English poetry rests on the heroic code, in which a generous lord and his loyal retainers are bound together, the men owe him loyalty to the death and then revenge, and kinship makes the nation. It uses kennings such as 'life-house' for the body, and alliteration rather than rhyme organizes the line. Its elegiac tone blends pagan heroism with Christianity, as in Beowulf and Caedmon's Hymn.

column1: How romance developed from Breton lays to Sir Gawain to Malory
column2: Celtic Breton lays, loved by Norman aristocrats, grew into chivalric romance, with its knightly quests, courtly love, courtesy and prowess. The Arthurian line runs from Geoffrey of Monmouth to Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, which survives in a single manuscript and belongs to the Alliterative Revival, and then to Malory's Morte Darthur, which Caxton printed in 1485.

column1: How the plague of 1348 led to social mobility
column2: The Black Death of 1348 killed one quarter to one third of Europe's population, so labor was scarce and people could move up socially. This produced a rising merchant class, for whom Chaucer, a merchant's son, wrote in English, along with social and religious criticism in Langland's Piers Plowman and in Wycliffe and the Lollards' English Bible. It also led to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

column1: How the Anglo-Saxons shaped Old English and its literature
column2: The Angles, Saxons and Jutes brought the Germanic speech that became Old English, the language of Caedmon's Hymn and Beowulf. Beowulf shows the heroic code, wergild and the elegiac tone, and Bede's Ecclesiastical History, which preserves Caedmon's Hymn, is partly hagiography.

column1: Sound and word-play in Old English poetry and the later return of alliteration
column2: In Old English alliterative verse any vowel alliterates with any other vowel, and poets also used synecdoche and metonymy, such as 'keel' for a ship and 'crown' for the king. The riddles of the Exeter Book, full of double entendre, show the Anglo-Saxon love of riddles. Alliterative verse came back in the 1300s in the Alliterative Revival, in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Piers Plowman.

column1: How Anglo-Saxon law and government shaped later English institutions
column2: Anglo-Saxon law replaced blood revenge with wergild, and failing to pay it brought dishonor, as Beowulf shows. Alfred the Great created the fyrd as the first national militia and was advised by the Witan, which later became William's Great Council and was a forerunner of Parliament. Each shire was run for the king by a shire-reeve, and that title is the origin of the word 'sheriff'.

column1: How English changed from Old English to Early Modern English
column2: After Old English came Middle English, the language Chaucer wrote in, which was not yet standardized. In the 1400s a London and East Midlands standard emerged, the Great Vowel Shift changed how long vowels sounded, and print fixed spelling, and together these moved Middle English toward Early Modern English, the language of Shakespeare.

column1: The mystery and morality plays of medieval English drama
column2: Medieval English drama included mystery plays, which were performed in cycles such as the York and Wakefield cycles, and morality plays, the best-known example being Everyman.
